lines.text: A particle can keep moving without a driving resultant force. Forces explain changes in motion, so start by identifying every force acting on the chosen body.

A force is an interaction measured in newtons. Newton's first law says a body stays at rest or continues at constant velocity if the resultant force is zero. For constant mass, Newton's second law is the sum of vector F equals m vector a, the acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force. In a plane, resolve the vector equation into i and j components. Newton's third law says two interacting bodies exert forces on each other that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. These forces act on different bodies, so only one belongs in either body's force equation.

Constant acceleration links the force model to the kinematics equations. Once a is found from the resultant force, use the appropriate equation of motion for the requested velocity, time or displacement.

Zero resultant force means constant velocity, including rest. the sum of vector F equals m vector a for constant mass. Third law partners act on different bodies. In a plane, resolve force and acceleration by components.
Why can two equal and opposite third law forces not cancel in the force equation for just one particle?
A string can make two particles move together, while a ground impact can suddenly change which forces act. Separate force diagrams and motion phases keep the model accurate.

For two particles joined by a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley or peg, a taut string gives the same acceleration magnitude to both and the same tension along the string. Choose a positive direction for each body and apply the sum of F equals m a separately. Add the equations to eliminate the internal tension, then substitute back to find it. On a plane inclined at theta to the horizontal, resolve weight into m g sine theta down the plane and m g cosine theta perpendicular to it. A smooth plane has no friction, on a rough plane include friction opposing the motion. If one particle hits the ground, use its velocity at that instant as the starting velocity for a new phase. Check whether the string becomes slack, then redraw the remaining forces and solve the later motion.
The acceleration from Newton's second law feeds into constant acceleration kinematics. At a force change, the velocity is carried across the phase boundary, while acceleration may change.

Draw a separate force diagram for each particle. A taut light string gives one tension and equal acceleration magnitudes. Resolve slope weight as m g sine theta parallel and m g cosine theta perpendicular. After impact, start a new force and kinematics phase.
Why can tension disappear when two connected particle equations are added, yet still be needed to find the tension itself?
During a brief collision, large contact forces act for a short time. Momentum and impulse describe the motion change without needing the detailed force history.

A particle's momentum is p equals m v, with velocity and momentum signed along the chosen one dimensional axis. Impulse is force times time for a constant force, or more generally the change in momentum, J equals m v minus m u. This is the impulse momentum principle. In a direct collision between two particles, their total momentum before equals their total momentum after when the resultant external impulse on the two particle system is negligible. Write both particles signed momenta before and after, then solve the resulting equation. If the particles stick, they share a final velocity. Do not assume kinetic energy conservation or use a restitution law, neither is required for these one dimensional questions.
Newton's second law connects force with momentum change. The collision equation treats both particles as one system, so their internal impulses cancel.

Momentum is signed, p equals m v. Impulse equals change in momentum, J equals m open bracket v minus u close bracket. Negligible external impulse gives conservation of total momentum. Direct collisions here are one dimensional, kinetic energy need not be conserved.
Why can total momentum be conserved when the two colliding particles exert large forces on each other?
A surface pushes perpendicular to itself and resists sliding along itself. On a slope, finding the perpendicular push is essential before calculating friction.

The normal reaction R acts perpendicular to the contact surface. The coefficient of friction mu relates the magnitude of friction to this reaction for a moving particle, F equals mu R. Friction acts opposite to the actual relative motion. On a horizontal surface without other vertical forces, R equals m g. On a plane inclined at theta with no other perpendicular force or acceleration, R equals m g cosine theta. Resolve forces along the plane after finding R. A particle sliding down has friction up the slope, a particle sliding up has friction down the slope. The formula describes friction during motion here, so do not replace it with a guess about direction or with R equals m g on an incline.
Use the resolved friction force in Newton's second law equation along the surface. The resulting acceleration can then be used in the constant acceleration equations.

For a moving particle, friction magnitude is F equals mu R. Friction opposes relative motion. Resolve perpendicular to find R, on a simple slope, R equals m g cosine theta. Then apply the sum of F equals m a along the surface.
Why does friction point down the plane when a particle is sliding upward?
Explain Newton's three laws and why an action reaction pair does not cancel in a single particle's equation.
Newton's first law describes zero resultant, the second gives the sum of vector F equals m vector a, and the third concerns equal opposite forces on different bodies.
Think about motion when the resultant is zero.
State the force acceleration equation.
Name which body receives each interaction force.
Two particles initially move on a taut string over a smooth pulley. One hits the ground while the other is still moving. Explain how to find the subsequent motion.
The force system changes at impact. The velocity is continuous through the instant, but the later acceleration must come from a new force diagram.
Split the motion at the impact instant.
Decide whether tension continues to act.
Use the impact velocity as the new initial velocity.
Explain when momentum may be conserved in a direct collision and why kinetic energy need not be conserved.
Internal collision impulses cancel for the system. This supports momentum conservation without assuming an elastic collision or a restitution rule.
Treat the two particles as one system.
Ask which impulses are external.
Keep velocity signs in the momentum equation.
A particle is sliding up a rough incline. Explain the direction and magnitude of friction and how the normal reaction is found.
Friction opposes sliding, so it points downhill here. Resolve perpendicular to the slope to obtain R, then use F equals mu R.
Use the actual direction of sliding.
Resolve perpendicular to the plane.
Use the coefficient only after finding the reaction.

Particles ay and B of masses three kilograms and five kilograms hang on a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Released from rest with the string taut, B falls one point two five metres before hitting the ground and remaining there. A stays clear of the pulley. Take g equals nine point eight metres per second squared. Calculate part a, the acceleration before contact, part b, the speed at contact, and part c, the further distance A rises before first coming to rest. Explain the change of force model.

Adding the taut string equations gives a equals two point four five metres per second squared and v equals the square root of six point one two five equals two point four seven metres per second. A continues upward and the string slackens, so T equals zero and its acceleration is g downward, its further rise is six point one two five over open bracket two g close bracket equals zero point three one two five metres, or zero point three one three metres.
Draw separate force diagrams before contact.
Use the fall distance to find the contact speed.
After contact, decide whether the rising particle keeps the string taut.

A four kilograms particle slides up a rough plane inclined at thirty degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is zero point two zero, no force other than weight and contact forces acts. Take g equals nine point eight metres per second squared. Calculate part a, the normal reaction and part b, the signed acceleration, taking up the plane as positive.

Perpendicular balance gives R equals four g cosine thirty degrees equals thirty three point nine newtons. Friction acts down the plane, so four a equals minus four g sine thirty degrees minus zero point two zero R and a equals minus six point six zero metres per second squared.
Resolve perpendicular to the plane first.
Friction opposes the upward sliding.
Both gravity along the plane and friction have negative components.

A two kilograms particle moves right at three metres per second and collides directly with a three kilograms particle moving left at four metres per second. They stick together, external impulse is negligible. Taking right as positive, calculate part a, their common velocity and state its direction, and part b, the signed impulse on the two kilograms particle.

Signed momentum gives two open bracket three close bracket plus three open bracket minus four close bracket equals five v, so v equals minus one point two zero metres per second, to the left. The impulse on the first particle is two open bracket minus one point two minus three close bracket equals minus eight point four zero newton seconds.
Give the initial leftward velocity a negative sign.
Use the combined mass after sticking.
For the impulse, use only the mass and velocity change of the specified particle.
A zero point five zero kilograms particle initially moves right at five metres per second and then moves left at three metres per second. Taking right as positive, calculate the impulse on it.

J equals zero point five zero open bracket minus three minus five close bracket equals minus four newton seconds. Subtracting speeds instead of signed velocities gives the incorrect minus one newton second, a positive impulse has the wrong direction.
Choose the signed final velocity.
Impulse is final momentum minus initial momentum.
The final velocity is negative and the initial velocity is positive.

The only forces on a two kilograms particle are open bracket eight i minus three j close bracket newtons and open bracket minus two i plus eleven j close bracket newtons. Calculate part a, the resultant force and part b, the acceleration vector.

Adding components gives vector F equals open bracket six i plus eight j close bracket newtons. Dividing each component by the mass gives vector a equals open bracket three i plus four j close bracket metres per second squared.
Add the force vectors component by component.
Apply Newton's second law to the resultant.
Divide both resultant components by the same mass.
A crate slides along a rough floor while a rope pulls it. State which pair of forces is a Newton's third law pair.
The floor pushes the crate and the crate pushes the floor, these are opposite forces from the same interaction on different bodies. Every other option names two forces acting on the crate.
Identify the body on which each force acts.
Third law partners belong to one interaction.
Swap the acting body and the receiving body to identify the partner.

A five kilograms particle slides right on a rough horizontal plane. A twenty newtons force acts rightward at angle alpha above the horizontal, where sine alpha equals three fifths and cosine alpha equals four fifths. The coefficient of friction is zero point two five. Take g equals nine point eight metres per second squared. Calculate part a, the normal reaction, part b, the friction magnitude and part c, the acceleration to the right.

Vertical balance gives R plus twenty open bracket three fifths close bracket equals forty nine, so R equals thirty seven newtons. Friction is zero point two five R equals nine point two five newtons leftward, hence five a equals twenty open bracket four fifths close bracket minus nine point two five and a equals one point three five metres per second squared.
Resolve the applied force horizontally and vertically.
There is no vertical acceleration, but the applied force changes the reaction.
Find friction from the reaction before writing the horizontal equation.
A particle slides up a rough incline, stops briefly, then slides back down. State the direction of friction while it is sliding in each phase, exclude the instant at rest.
Moving friction opposes the relative sliding, downhill during ascent and uphill during descent. Its direction is determined by velocity, so it reverses when the sliding direction reverses.
Consider the two sliding phases separately.
Identify the velocity direction in each phase.
Place friction opposite the relative velocity along the plane.
four Dynamics of a particle moving in a straight line or plane.
In one breath.

A resultant force changes a particle's velocity according to Newton's laws. Force diagrams, signed directions and separate motion phases turn connected particles, inclines, friction and collisions into equations.
Key ideas.

A force is a push or pull on a body, measured in newtons. Newton's first law says a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity when its resultant force is zero. The second law, for constant mass, is the sum of vector F equals m vector a, acceleration follows the resultant force. In a plane, apply this separately to the i and j components. Newton's third law says interacting bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other. The pair acts on different bodies, so it does not cancel in one body's force equation.

For connected particles joined by a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley or peg, the taut string has one tension and the particles share an acceleration magnitude. Draw a separate force diagram for each, tension cancels when the equations are added. If a particle hits the ground, find its velocity at contact, then set up a new force equation for any later motion. The string may become slack.

On an inclined plane at angle theta, weight has component m g sine theta down the plane and m g cosine theta into it. Without other perpendicular forces, the normal reaction is R equals m g cosine theta. A smooth plane has no friction. On a rough surface, a moving particle experiences friction of magnitude F equals mu R, opposing its motion. This coefficient of friction rule applies while the particle slides, do not assume friction points downhill.

The diagram shows a particle sliding up the plane, towards the upper right, friction F therefore points down the plane. Weight m g is vertical and R is perpendicular to the surface. Resolve weight as m g sine theta down the plane and m g cosine theta into it when writing equations, these are components of weight, not two extra forces.

Momentum is p equals m v and has the sign of velocity along a chosen line. Impulse is J equals delta p equals m open bracket v minus u close bracket, the impulse momentum principle. For a direct collision between two particles with negligible external impulse, total signed momentum before equals total signed momentum after. Kinetic energy need not be conserved, and no restitution law is needed here. Use g equals nine point eight metres per second squared throughout.

For a constant resultant force acting for time t, J equals F t equals m open bracket v minus u close bracket. Impulse has units newton seconds equals kilogram metres per second, keep the sign of force and velocity along the chosen axis.
Source, learner's library, Save My Exams, sources or library or SaveMyExams or XMA01 mechanics one or XMA01 c3.4. pdf, p.3, paraphrased.
Method.
Choose positive axes, draw forces on each particle, and resolve any sloping weight into parallel and perpendicular components.
Write the sum of F equals m a separately for each body. For a taut string, use the same acceleration magnitude and one tension.
Solve simultaneously. If forces change at impact, carry the contact velocity into a second phase and solve again.
For an impulse or collision, write signed initial and final momenta before substituting values. State the final direction.

For example, taking right as positive, a zero point five zero kilograms particle changing from plus four to minus two metres per second receives J equals zero point five zero open bracket minus two minus four close bracket equals minus three point zero newton seconds. If a constant resultant acts for zero point two zero seconds, F equals J over t equals minus fifteen newtons, the force acts leftward.
Worked example.

A two kilograms mass and a three kilograms mass hang over a smooth pulley. Find their acceleration and tension. Take the three kilograms mass downward as positive and the two kilograms mass upward as positive. Both have acceleration magnitude a. three g minus T equals three a, T minus two g equals two a. Add the equations, g equals five a, so a equals one point nine six metres per second squared. Substitute into T minus two g equals two a, T equals twenty three point five two newtons, or twenty three point five newtons to three significant figures.
Worked example, after ground contact.

In the preceding system, release the particles from rest with the heavier mass two point five metres above the ground. It stays on the ground after contact, the lighter mass remains clear of the pulley. Before contact, a equals one point nine six metres per second squared, so v squared equals two open bracket one point nine six close bracket times two point five equals nine point eight and the contact speed is three point one three metres per second. The lighter mass continues upward, shortening the distance from itself to the pulley while the heavier mass stays still. The string slackens, so T equals zero, only weight acts on the lighter mass. Its new acceleration is minus nine point eight metres per second squared, taking upward as positive. Its further rise follows from zero equals v squared minus two g h, h equals nine point eight over open bracket two times nine point eight close bracket equals zero point five zero metres. The old tension equation no longer applies because a slack string cannot pull, carry the lighter mass's velocity across the transition, not its acceleration.

Scope checked against Pearson Edexcel I ay L Mathematics specification, Unit M one, section four, forces may change after ground contact. Moving friction wording also checked against the learner's sources or library or SaveMyExams or XMA01 mechanics one or XMA01 c3.3. pdf, p.8.
Traps.
Trap, A body must have a forward resultant to keep moving. Why it's wrong, Zero resultant means constant velocity. Instead, Ask whether velocity is changing.
Trap, Use R equals m g on every slope. Why it's wrong, The perpendicular weight component is m g cosine theta. Instead, Resolve perpendicular to the plane first.
Trap, Treat action and reaction as cancelling on one particle. Why it's wrong, They act on different bodies. Instead, Draw one force diagram per particle.
Trap, Assume kinetic energy is conserved in every collision. Why it's wrong, Energy may change form. Instead, Use conservation of signed momentum when external impulse is negligible.
Exam technique.

For Calculate and Find, show the force or momentum equation before substitution, keep signs consistent and give units. For Explain, name the relevant law and the bodies or direction involved. Give numerical answers to two or three significant figures after using g equals nine point eight metres per second squared.
